results.content:
Hadrian secures $1.37 billion in funding at a $7.87 billion valuation as investor interest in defense manufacturing infrastructure grows.
Growing investor interest in defense supply chain capacity is driving fresh capital into companies focused on military production infrastructure. Hadrian says it has secured a new $1.37 billion funding round at a $7.87 billion valuation, lifting its total funding to about $2 billion.
Hadrian opened its fourth facility in Alabama in March, a $2.4 billion public-private partnership to mass-produce submarine parts and expand automated defense manufacturing. As reported by TechCrunch, Hadrian announced on Thursday that the round includes lead investors WCM Investment Management, Washington Harbour Partners, Valor Equity Partners, 137 Ventures and Baillie Gifford. Other participants include 1789 Capital, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, funds managed by Apollo and T.
Founders Fund and Lux previously led Hadrian’s $260 million Series C financing about a year earlier, and PitchBook estimates the company’s total capital raised now stands at roughly $2 billion. Rather than developing new AI-powered weapons, Hadrian focuses on automated factories designed to mass-produce parts used in existing military vehicles and systems.
Hadrian is already extending that model through new production sites tied to defense programs. In March, the company opened an Alabama facility to mass-produce submarine parts, marking its fourth facility.

results.name: Hadrian raises $1.37bn to accelerate automated US factories | TechFinitive
results.content:
# Hadrian raises $1.37bn to accelerate automated US factories  
Defence tech company [Hadrian](https://www.hadrian.co/) has raised $1.37bn in Series D funding to expand its network of highly automated US factories. The company is betting that software, robotics and skilled workers will help close persistent production gaps in defence and aerospace supply chains. This latest funding round values the company at $7.87bn.  
The financing round was co-led by WCM Investment Management, Washington Harbour Partners, Valor Equity Partners, 137 Ventures and Baillie Gifford. JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group came in as an anchor co-lead through its Security and Resiliency Initiative, while a raft of investors including CapitalG, Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux Capital, Apollo and T. Rowe Price also participated.  
Rather than develop another AI-enabled weapons platform, Hadrian’s strategy is building factories designed to manufacture precision components and eventually complete systems for existing aerospace and defence programmes. That is a much less glamorous layer of defence technology, perhaps, but one where bottlenecks have become painfully visible.  
The problem is production.
## Targeting industrial capacity  
According to the company, the new capital will fund additional factories, research and development, and production capabilities for mission-critical systems. Its “Factories-as-a-Service” model is intended to rapidly add capacity for priority areas such as munitions and shipbuilding.  
Hadrian now operates four sites across nearly 3m square feet: two facilities in Torrance, California, alongside new factories in Mesa, Arizona, and Muscle Shoals, Alabama. Further sites and new lines for munitions and autonomous systems are planned over the next year.  
That expansion reflects an important shift in industrial AI. While initiatives such as [Siemens and IFS’ work on the industrial AI loop](https://www.techfinitive.com/siemens-and-ifs-join-forces-to-close-the-industrial-ai-loop/) focus on linking operational data and engineering processes, Hadrian is applying the technology directly to factory throughput, routing and production execution.
## A defence manufacturing bet  
Hadrian uses its proprietary Opus software alongside automation and robotics to augment human workers in aerospace and defence manufacturing. It counts Lockheed Martin, RTX and Anduril among its customers. The US Navy also selected the company in March to mass-produce components in Alabama for Virginia-class attack and Columbia-class ballistic-missile submarines.  
The raise follows a [$260m Series C](https://www.hadrian.co/blog/series-c) roughly a year ago, taking Hadrian’s total funding to about $2bn.  
The premise is straightforward: deterrence depends not only on designs or stockpiles, but on the ability to produce at speed. As [agentic manufacturing gains traction](https://www.techfinitive.com/features/schneider-electric-at-hannover-messe-2026-agentic-manufacturing-goes-mainstream/), Hadrian’s funding round shows investors increasingly see automated factory capacity as strategic infrastructure rather than a back-office efficiency project.

results.content:
Prior to this latest funding, Hadrian had already demonstrated a significant ability to attract capital. The company raised $90 million in its Series A round in 2022, followed by a $117 million Series B in 2023 [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/). The Series B round alone had established Hadrian as a unicorn, valuing the company at $1 billion [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/). The leap from a $1 billion valuation to $8 billion in less than a year underscores an aggressive growth trajectory and intense investor confidence in its capabilities and market execution.
## FAQ  
**Q: What is Hadrian's primary mission?** A: Hadrian's primary mission is to modernize the defense sector's manufacturing capabilities by leveraging advanced technologies such as AI, automation, and advanced robotics. The company focuses on rapidly producing precision machined parts for critical defense applications, addressing supply chain bottlenecks [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/).  
**Q: How much funding did Hadrian secure in its latest round, and what is its valuation?** A: Hadrian secured $1.37 billion in its Series C funding round, bringing its post-money valuation to $8 billion [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/).  
**Q: Who were the lead investors in Hadrian's Series C round?** A: The Series C funding round for Hadrian was led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z). Other significant investors included Lux Capital, Founders Fund, and RTX Ventures [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/).  
**Q: What types of products does Hadrian manufacture?** A: Hadrian manufactures precision machined parts for critical defense applications, including components for satellites, hypersonic missiles, and advanced aircraft [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/).
**Q: How quickly did Hadrian's valuation grow?** A: Hadrian's valuation grew significantly, reaching $1 billion in its Series B round in 2023, and then jumping to $8 billion in its Series C round in 2026. This represents an eight-fold increase in valuation in less than a year [TechCrunch, 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/06/defense-tech-hadrian-raises-1-37b-at-8b-valuation/).
